I adore all the solo albums to be very clear, but I’m a sucker for a strong theme/storyline. It doesn’t mean they have to write or produce it themselves or that it needs to come from a “dark” place for it to stick out for me. One of the reasons Layover is my top album from the solo era is because it just feels complete, like all the songs belong to one singular body of work. I think “love” wasn’t a strong connection point for me with Golden, but he showed himself as a skillful singer, a complete pop-star, and thoroughly entertaining. With Happy, I once again loved all the songs individually but they didn’t necessarily come under the same umbrella or flow conceptually. Muse, to your point, showed us so much more of Jimin’s versatility but I didn’t necessarily understand what he was sharing. I’ll take your points about it though, maybe I needed a new perspective to bond with it again.

Fair enough. I understand we're a diverse fandom with diverse opinions, so I thought putting it as "largely" was enough of a preface that I don't mean the whole fandom, of course. As a big fan of the album, I've voraciously consumed any big discussion thread or post by ARMYs about said album, so my observation was mainly from that. 

Sonical cohesion is an interesting concept, and i think people's interpretations vary. So I understand how some may not agree with it being cohesive. While some people interpret it as songs sounding similar or not too diverse genre-wise, others interpret it as songs flowing well from one to the next even if they sound different. I belong to the latter category, which is why it's cohesive *to me*. As I listen to the album top to bottom, there is no track that is jarring and takes me out of my immersion. I think No. 29 plays a big role in providing a breathing space too.

Part 1, before the bell, discussing roots, longing/sorrow, separation/alienation, resilience (han) and part 2, after the bell, focusing on reunion, belonging, joy and energy/celebration (heung). Sonically, I like how  two parts mirror the lyrical concepts, with part 1 having heavy beats and intense energy, and part 2 having a lighter, melodic feel and energy. Incorporating traditional Korean instruments and sounds really brings it home/elevates it, imo.

The cool thing for me is that this exploration then gives me this overall sense of identity/togetherness. Between themselves and between them and ARMY: this is who we are, and this is our bond. Kind of like 'jeong' almost, but perhaps not quite   
And that, in turn, brings me joy.

(side note: it was so interesting and joyful to see this being brought to life in their concert. From the Korean instrumental music before the concert even starts, to the imagery on stage and on the screens, and the entire stadium singing Arirang, to name just a few things, it's the album brought to visual life. I wish I could have attended more than just two concerts)

I'm also baby army, so not who this is directed toward, but Hybe Boy on YouTube has excellent English-language translations of Lives, interviews, and other stuff going back several years.
